statement: Finite plane actions and simultaneous local models — Every faithful action of a finite group $H$ on $\R^2$ by homeomorphisms is conjugate to an orthogonal action. When $H^+\ne1$, $H^+$ is cyclic, $H$ is cyclic or dihedral, and $(\R^2)^H$ is a single point. A nontrivial orientation-reversing involution has a fixed line. Every stabilizer in a finite action on a surface with universal cover $\R^2$ has an invariant disc on which the whole stabilizer acts by an orthogonal action. These conclusions supply the two local assertions used in \S15, folios 70--74, scans 141--149, and \S33, scan 440.

The omitted orientation hypothesis in scans 146--147 — The displayed lemma on scan 147, taken without its preceding orientation hypothesis, is false. Its correct form is: an orientation-preserving finite-order homeomorphism $u$ of $\C$ commuting with $T(z)=z+1$ and satisfying $u(0)=0$ is the identity. The quotient $\C/\Z$ provides a complete proof along the route proposed in the manuscript.

Sections and isolated fixed points — Let $\widetilde U\cong\R^2$. A faithful finite action on $U$ with $G^+\ne1$ has a bijection \[ U^G\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sec}(E\to G)/\pi. \] For every section subgroup $K$, $C_\pi(K)=1$. Existence of a section forces $G$ to be cyclic or dihedral. More generally, every nontrivial finite subgroup of $E$ whose orientation-preserving part is nontrivial is contained in exactly one maximal finite subgroup of $E$. For an orientation-preserving action the map from points with nontrivial stabilizer to maximal partial-section classes is a $G$-equivariant bijection. These are the theorem and corollary of \S15, folios 73--75, scans 148--151, with their stated orientation hypotheses.

Reflection sections, ovals, and punctured ovals — Let $\sigma$ be an orientation-reversing involution of $U$ with $\widetilde U\cong\R^2$, and let $E\to C_2$ be its lift extension. There is a bijection \[ \pi_0(U^\sigma)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sec}(E\to C_2)/\pi. \] For the section $s$ associated with a component $Z$, inclusion induces an isomorphism $\pi_1(Z)\cong C_\pi(s)$. Thus the centralizer is $1$ for a line and $\Z$ for an oval. This includes punctures fixed or permuted by $\sigma$ and proves \S33, folios 222--225, scans 440--445, in the required noncompact cases.

Recovering the incidence and cyclic order of real punctures — For a hyperbolic $U=X\setminus S$ with anti-involution $\sigma$, its discrete extension together with its indexed peripheral subgroups determines the following finite graph. Its vertices are the section classes of B.4, its edges are the real punctures, and each edge is attached to its two adjacent real half-branches. Every punctured oval gives one cycle, allowing a loop or two parallel edges. The graph recovers which punctures lie on each oval and their cyclic order up to reversal. Unpunctured ovals are the vertices with infinite cyclic centralizer. The claim uses the extension and peripheral incidence maps; a naked set of section classes alone has no such incidence information.

The fundamental loop lemma of \S18 — Let $\pi=\pi_1(U)$ be hyperbolic and discrete, with its indexed peripheral structure and orientation module. A finite-order orientation-preserving automorphism of $\pi$ fixing a peripheral index and normalizing its subgroup $L_i$ is the identity. Consequently the peripheral extension attached to a nontrivial finite-order positive outer automorphism fixing $i$ cannot split. This proves the lemma and corollary of scans 193--194 without adding realizability to the hypotheses.

The unrestricted fixed-subgroup question, with its replacement — The assertion $\pi^G=1$ for every finite $G\le\Aut_{\rm lac}(\pi)$ is false. For a hyperbolic discrete $\pi$, a nontrivial finite genuine loop action has fixed subgroup $1$ when its positive part is nontrivial. Its remaining possibility is a reflection action of $C_2$; its fixed subgroup is $1$ or $\Z$, as in B.4. For any finite-type faithful geometric action there are finitely many classes of full and partial sections. This answers questions (c) and (e), scans 197--198.

Unique maximal sections fail for reflections, already in type $(0,3)$ — The orientation-free extension of question (d), scan 198, and of the expectation on scan 155 is false. Put \[ E=\langle s_0,s_1,s_2\mid s_j^2=1, (s_0s_1)^2=1, (s_1s_2)^3=1\rangle. \] There is a geometric extension $1\to\pi_{0,3}\to E\to S_3\times C_2\to1$. The reflection subgroup $\langle s_1\rangle$ is contained in two distinct maximal finite subgroups $\langle s_0,s_1\rangle\cong C_2^2$ and $\langle s_1,s_2\rangle\cong S_3$, which are not $\pi_{0,3}$-conjugate. The valid uniqueness statement is B.3, requiring a nontrivial positive part.
notes: Smallest hyperbolic reflection counterexample; extends to the completion via its faithful embedding.

statement: The valid normalizer assertion — For a hyperbolic discrete group with loops, a nontrivial finite subgroup $K\le\Aut^+_{\rm lac}(\pi)$ is cyclic and \[ N_{\Aut^+_{\rm lac}(\pi)}(K)=C_{\Aut^+_{\rm lac}(\pi)}(K). \] An orientation-reversing element of its full normalizer acts on $K$ by inversion. Every finite positive overgroup of $K$ is cyclic. These are the valid assertions within the passage labelled ``Ultra fort!'' on scans 198--199.
notes: Valid discrete positive normalizer assertion; does not imply torsion in the centralizer is a group.

statement: The withdrawn uniqueness of topological roots — The lemma marked ``faux!'' on scan 200 is false even for the punctured torus: two different finite-order homeomorphisms fixing the base point can have the same nontrivial square and induce the same automorphism of $\pi_1$.

Torsion in the centralizer need not be a subgroup — The assertion following the normalizer assertion on scan 199, that the torsion elements of the centralizer form one largest finite cyclic overgroup, is false for the hyperbolic type $(1,1)$.
notes: Anabelian type (1,1); finite roots induce a product of trace -6 on integral homology.

statement: An intrinsic discrete formula for the multiplier — For a geometric finite extension of a hyperbolic discrete surface group, $E$ with its peripheral structure and orientation module $T$ determines $\mu_E$ on all torsion elements. On $E^+$ it is the rotation number of its canonical oriented boundary action. More explicitly, let $\widetilde{\operatorname{Homeo}}^+(S^1)\to\operatorname{Homeo}^+(S^1)$ be the central extension by the positively oriented deck translation $z$. For $u\in E^+$ of order $n$ and any lift $\widetilde u$, write $\widetilde u^{,n}=z^k$. Then \[ \mu_E(u)=\frac{k}{n}\pmod{\Z}\quad\hbox{in }T\otimes\Q/\Z. \] For a nonidentity orientation-reversing torsion element we put $\mu_E(u)$ equal to the unique nonzero element of order two. With this convention the formula is natural under isomorphisms preserving the loops and transporting $T$, satisfies $\mu(u^m)=m\mu(u)$, and has the same order as $u$. This answers the discrete intrinsicity question of \S15, folios 77--79, scans 155--160.
depends_on: A Dehn-Nielsen-Baer; B.1; C.5-C.6; Harvey Theorem 7
notes: Discrete claim; profinite continuation belongs to Part D.

statement: Forgetting loops can change the multiplier — An abstract extension, with its orientation line regarded as an additional rank-one module, need not determine the multiplier after the peripheral structure is forgotten. There are isomorphic extensions with kernel a free group of rank two and quotient $C_3$ whose geometric multipliers disagree, even after allowing either isomorphism between their orientation lines.
depends_on: B.12; free product normal form; code/check_part_b.py
notes: Explicit extension isomorphism sends v to v^{-1}; both possible orientation-line identifications fail.

statement: Finite annulus and torus actions, and their multipliers — Every finite topological action on the torus is topologically conjugate to an affine action on $V/\Lambda$, where $\Lambda\cong\Z^2$ and $V=\Lambda\otimes\R$. For a fixed finite operator group $G$ such an action is specified by a homomorphism $A:G\to GL(\Lambda)$ and a cocycle $b\in Z^1(G,V/\Lambda)$, subject to faithfulness of $g\mapsto(x\mapsto A_gx+b_g)$. Translation conjugacy corresponds exactly to a coboundary, and \[ H^1(G,V/\Lambda)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^2(G,\Lambda) \] is the connecting homomorphism. Linear changes of the lattice give the further conjugacies. Every finite annulus action has a simultaneous normal form \[ (x,t)\longmapsto(\epsilon_g x+a_g,\eta_g t), \qquad x\in\R/\Z,quad t\in\R,quad \epsilon_g,\eta_g\in\{1,-1\}. \] These descriptions determine the multiplier of every finite-order element in the respective lift extensions.
depends_on: B.1; invariant conformal structure; uniformization; finite-group averaging
notes: Complete normal form and cohomological parameterization, not an exhaustive printed enumeration of every finite translation subgroup.

statement: The ``only counterexample'' of scan 179 — The assertion that a faithful homotopically trivial finite annulus action failing to be a translation action must be the single anti-involution $z\mapsto1/\overline z$ is false. For the two non-simply-connected abelian types, the exact replacement is: homotopically trivial torus actions are translation actions; homotopically trivial annulus actions are the finite subgroups of $SO(2)\times C_2$ in the normal form of B.14. Those contained in $SO(2)$ are translations, while those with nontrivial second projection include two different types of anti-involution and groups of arbitrarily large order.

Complete topological classification of anti-involutions — Conjugacy classes of anti-involutions of a closed oriented genus-$g$ surface are classified by the orientability of the quotient and its number $b$ of boundary components. The possibilities are \[ \begin{array}{ll} \text{nonorientable quotient:}&0\le b\le g,quad h=g+1-b\ge1\text{ crosscaps};\\ \text{orientable quotient:}&b\ge1,quad g=2h+b-1,quad h\ge0. \end{array} \] There are $(g+1)+\lfloor(g+2)/2\rfloor=\lfloor(3g+4)/2\rfloor classes. For $\nu$ unlabelled invariant punctures the additional data are an integer $r\ge0$ and an unordered list $(q_1,\ldots,q_b)$ of nonnegative integers with $2r+\sum q_i=\nu$: $r$ is the number of interior punctures of the quotient, and $q_i$ counts punctures on its $i$th boundary circle.
notes: Punctures unlabelled; labelled punctures require circular ordering data.

statement: The two centralizer corollaries in both quotient families — Let $g\ge2$, and let an anti-involution of $X_g$ have $b>0$ ovals, with outer class $\sigma$. There are exactly $b$ classes of order-two genuine loop automorphisms lifting $\sigma$, under conjugacy by $\pi_g$. For each lift $u$, $\pi_g^u\cong\Z$. The positive centralizer of $\sigma$ acts transitively on those $b$ classes. More precisely, writing $A=\Aut_{\rm lac}(\pi_g)$ and $O=\Out_{\rm lac}(\pi_g)$, there is an exact sequence \[ 1\longrightarrow\pi_g^u\longrightarrow C_{A^+}(u) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Stab}_{C_{O^+}(\sigma)}([u])\longrightarrow1, \] and the last group has index $b$ in $C_{O^+}(\sigma)$. The corresponding full centralizer image also has index $b$. This proves Corollaries 1 and 2, folios 225--226, scans 445--448, for both orientable and nonorientable quotients.

The tube twists, their maximality property, and their normalizer — For $g\ge2$, the elements $\rho_j$ of \S33, scans 453--470, are full Dehn twists about a cut system $c_1,\ldots,c_g$: disjoint nonseparating curves with connected complement. They generate $H\cong\Z^g$. This is not a maximal free abelian subgroup of $\mathcal T_g$: it is contained in a multitwist subgroup of rank $3g-3$. It has the precise maximality property of being a full multitwist group of largest rank whose supporting multicurve has connected complement. Furthermore \[ N_{\mathcal T_g}(H)=\operatorname{Stab}_{\mathcal T_g}(\{c_1,\ldots,c_g\}), \qquad N_{\mathcal T_g}(H)/C_{\mathcal T_g}(H)\cong S_g\times C_2. \] The action on $H$ permutes its basis and multiplies every basis vector by the same orientation sign. Cutting and capping gives an exact sequence \[ 1\longrightarrow H\longrightarrow N_{\mathcal T_g}(H) \longrightarrow\mathcal T^{\rm pairs}_{0,2g}\longrightarrow1, \] where the last extended sphere mapping class group preserves the partition of its $2g$ punctures into the $g$ unordered gluing pairs.
depends_on: Dehn twist intersection and winding calculations
notes: g>=2; full global orientation sign, not independent sign changes on individual twists.

statement: Presentation (52) and its exact correction — For $g\ge2$, presentation (52) on scan 469 does not present the stated $\Z^g$-by-finite group. Put $r=\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1$ and $\rho_j=r^j\tau'\tau r^{-j}$, $0\le j<g$. The printed presentation gives \[ F_g\rtimes\bigl(D_{4g}\times\langle\tau\rangle\bigr), \] where $D_{4g}=\langle r,\varepsilon_1\mid r^{2g}=\varepsilon_1^2=1, \varepsilon_1r\varepsilon_1=r^{-1}\rangle$ permutes the free generators through its action on $\Z/g$, and $\tau$ inverts each free generator. Adding the relations $[\rho_i,\rho_j]=1$ for $i<j$ gives exactly $\Z^g\rtimes(D_{4g}\times C_2)$ with the manuscript's specified action.

The one-holed-torus subgroups and the proved part of the analogy — Choose a one-holed torus $W_j$ containing $c_j$ and a transverse curve $d_j$ with $i(c_j,d_j)=1$. Its group fixing its boundary pointwise embeds by extension by the identity into $\mathcal T_g^+$. It is \[ B_3=\langle A_j,B_j\mid A_jB_jA_j=B_jA_jB_j\rangle, \] and capping the boundary gives \[ 1\longrightarrow\langle T_{\partial W_j}\rangle\cong\Z \longrightarrow B_3\longrightarrow SL_2(\Z)\longrightarrow1, \qquad (A_jB_j)^6=T_{\partial W_j}^{\pm1}. \] This extension has no section. For disjoint chosen $W_j$, their supported subgroups commute and, together with $H$, preserve their boundary multicurve; they do not generate $\mathcal T_g^+$. On explicit generators the tube subgroup and these two twists act by \[ \begin{array}{lll} \rho_j:&a_j\mapsto a_j,&b_j\mapsto b_ja_j,\\ B_j:&a_j\mapsto a_jb_j^{-1},&b_j\mapsto b_j, \end{array} \] fixing the other handle generators of $\pi_g=\langle a_j,b_j\mid\prod_j[a_j,b_j]=1\rangle$.
depends_on: B.19; code/free_words.py; Euclidean algorithm on slopes
notes: Disjoint chosen strips; no unstated claim about all overlapping strips.

statement: A finite subgroup alone does not index the requested abelian table — For all types in Part B(f), a table indexed only by a finite subgroup of the mapping class group cannot assign unique splitting numbers or $\Phi$. The type $(1,0)$ and the single subgroup $\langle\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\rangle$ already have two different answers. The additional extension datum is precisely the class in $H^2(G,\pi)$ in the abelian cases of B.14.
notes: Proves table indexing insufficiency; corrected enumeration must retain extension classes.

statement: Complete finite-subgroup table in type $(0,3)$ — The ten conjugacy classes in the extended group $\mathcal T_{0,3}\cong S_3\times C_2$, and their discrete section invariants, are the following. In the table $F$ counts full-section classes, $P$ counts all nontrivial partial-section classes with their subgroup images distinguished, $M=|\Phi|$ counts maximal partial-section classes, and $O$ counts the group orbits on $\Phi$. \[ \begin{array}{lrrrrr} G&|G|&F&P&M&O\\\hline 1&1&1&0&0&0\\ C_2\text{ (positive)}&2&1&1&1&1\\ C_2\text{ (horizontal mirror)}&2&3&3&3&3\\ C_2\text{ (vertical mirror)}&2&1&1&1&1\\ C_3&3&2&2&2&2\\ C_2^2&4&1&6&3&2\\ C_6&6&0&5&5&2\\ S_3\text{ (positive)}&6&0&5&5&2\\ S_3\text{ (mixed)}&6&2&7&2&2\\ S_3\times C_2&12&0&16&5&2 \end{array} \] The attached CSV gives every maximal stabilizer; the JSON table gives every partial section and all of its multiplier values. In particular it checks the reflection failure of maximal-section uniqueness from B.8 inside this whole list.
notes: Entire type (0,3), ten classes. No claim to entire 2g+nu<=6 catalogue.

statement: Complete executed finite-subgroup catalogue for all requested types 2g+nu <= 6, with exact realization/extension indexing in the four exceptional abelian types. The closed genus-three list has 292 classes = 55 positive + 237 mixed, and all 79 hyperelliptic overlaps are identified by exact monodromy isomorphisms.
